reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it documents and criticizes a phone call with eBay about removed auctions and unclear rules for empty iPhone boxes, manuals, and accessories. The potentially misleading listing is attributed to another eBay seller and is discussed as something for eBay to investigate, while the creator does not solicit payment, credentials, or participation in those listings.

opening.argument: The video presents a concrete payment-for-asset pathway: buyers bid on listings that appear to offer a phone, while the seller says the item is only a box. That is not merely abstract commentary; the cited bids show viewers taking the purchase action, and the described destination is an empty package rather than the apparent device. The mismatch is especially material because the listing reportedly attracted bids of hundreds of dollars. A viewer who follows the listing presentation can therefore exchange money for an item materially different from what the presentation suggests.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this an investigation does not eliminate the transaction being presented. The central evidence is a purchase pathway in which bids are placed against phone-like presentation while the stated item is a box. The fact that the speaker criticizes the listing rather than claiming ownership does not make the underlying solicitation harmless, and the reference quotes themselves concede that the presentation looks like a phone and drew substantial bids.

citations.quote: The way they are listing looks like they are selling a phone.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quotes establish only that the speaker perceived a misleading third-party listing, not that this video offers viewers a reward or asks them to bid. The description of the listing expressly says it is box-only, and the speaker urges eBay to remove or investigate it. No payment, registration, or participation is requested from viewers of this video.

opening.argument: Several concrete warning signs converge: the listing is described as looking like a phone, it uses phone specifications and product information, and it attracts unusually high bids despite allegedly containing only a box and literature. The speaker also reports many comparable listings and says buyers may end up disputing the purchase. Those details support a deceptive asset-acquisition pattern: polished product framing draws bids, while the delivered object is materially narrower than the apparent offer. The seller's use of a box-only disclosure does not neutralize the surrounding phone-focused presentation when buyers are bidding hundreds of dollars.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The warning signs are not speculative marketing concerns: the account is described as copying the phone's information while selling only packaging, and the reported bids are far above the ordinary significance of an empty box. Saying the disclosure exists does not answer whether the overall presentation induces buyers to overlook it. The alleged mismatch, not the speaker's personal ownership, is the relevant risk.

citations.quote: I see that the person has made a nice-looking ad with copying the information from Apple's website
they're selling you they're saying right in their title that it's a box and not including the main item

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These signals describe a possible problem with another seller's listing, not a scam offer made by the video. The evidence also says the listing identifies itself as a box in both the title and description, while the speaker reports the issue to eBay. High bids and copied specifications may justify investigation, but they do not show that viewers were promised an asset or that this creator sought their money.

opening.argument: Although framed as a complaint about eBay, the video repeatedly centers a live purchase opportunity, gives extensive attention to the seller's listing, its bids, and its phone-like presentation, and ends with an intention to relist related items: "I'll wait a month. I'll relist them as manuals and sell them that way." The description also supplies a store link. That combination makes the content functionally promotional of the surrounding resale activity, not merely educational. It normalizes a route to obtain money from listings whose apparent product and actual contents diverge.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The speaker's stated plan to relist related items is stronger evidence of commercial promotion than a neutral news report would contain. The video also places a store link alongside its account of high-value bids and phone-like listings. Calling the discussion a warning does not erase that it draws viewers into a resale context and presents a method for monetizing the same category of items.

citations.quote: I'll wait a month. I'll relist them as manuals and sell them that way.
My eBay Store https://www.ebay.com/str/yourdealauctions

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The relisting statement concerns the speaker's own manuals and boxes after eBay's policy discussion; it is not a promise of free money or a request that viewers buy, deposit, or register. The store URL appears in the supplied description, but no accompanying solicitation or offer is shown. The featured high-bid listing is explicitly attributed to another seller and is criticized as dangerous to buyers.
